facts.headline: The Bean has no seams — on purpose
facts.body_html: Anish Kapoor's 110-ton Cloud Gate is welded together from 168 stainless steel plates and polished until every seam disappeared — the mirror finish took over two years to perfect.

facts.headline: Chicago engineers reversed an entire river
facts.body_html: In 1900, the city blasted open a new canal and made the Chicago River flow backward — away from Lake Michigan instead of into it — so its own sewage would stop poisoning the city's drinking water.

facts.headline: These glass boxes hang 1,353 feet over nothing
facts.body_html: The Ledge at Willis Tower puts you inside a glass balcony 4.3 feet off the building, floating a quarter-mile above the street with only 1.5 inches of glass underfoot.
suggested_queries: Willis Tower Ledge glass box Chicago

facts.headline: Wrigley's scoreboard has never gone digital
facts.body_html: Built in 1937, Wrigley Field's centerfield scoreboard is still flipped by hand from the inside — and the outfield ivy planted that same year remains the only living wall in Major League Baseball.

facts.headline: Chicago's 'corncobs' park cars in a spiral
facts.body_html: Marina City's twin towers wrap their bottom 19 floors into an exposed spiral parking ramp — when they opened in 1964, they were the tallest reinforced-concrete structures on Earth.

facts.headline: Nobody knows what the Picasso downtown actually is
facts.body_html: Picasso gave this 50-foot, 162-ton sculpture to Chicago for free in 1967 and never said what it depicts — guesses range from his Afghan hound to a woman's profile hidden in the curves.

facts.headline: One tower walked through the fire that burned the city down
facts.body_html: When the Great Chicago Fire leveled the city in 1871, the Water Tower's yellow Joliet limestone walls didn't burn — it's one of the only structures left standing from before the fire.
